title: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
hookLine: the master reciter, whom the Prophet ﷺ was told to recite to (Bukhari)

lines: TODAY: I WAS TOLD TO RECITE TO YOU.
cards: God has commanded me to recite to you. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it to a man in Medina. Not to the whole community.
To you. Yesterday a companion recited to the Prophet; today it runs the other way, and it's stranger. The man is Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and his first question isn't about the surah.
It's one breathless question about himself. Today: Ubayy.

teach.h: ONE OF THE ANSAR, A SCRIBE.
teach.b: Ubayy ibn Ka'b was one of the Ansar, the people of Medina, and he wrote down revelation for the Prophet. In the short list of people to learn the Qur'an from, the one we met yesterday, his name is there too.

teach.h: GOD COMMANDED ME TO RECITE TO YOU.
teach.b: The Prophet says to him: God has commanded me to recite to you the surah that begins Lam yakun, the one known as al-Bayyinah, the Clear Proof.
And Ubayy asks: did He name me? Yes, the Prophet says. And Ubayy weeps.
He knows the Qur'an deeply; he could recite this surah himself. In the report, what brings the tears is not the surah. It is being named, and having the words carried to him personally.

A second scene, in Sahih Muslim, shows the other side of him. The Prophet tests him: which verse in the book of God that you have with you is the greatest? Ubayy answers: the verse of the Throne, Ayat al-Kursi.
And the Prophet strikes him on the chest and says, may knowledge delight you. A man who knew the text well enough to be quizzed, and who still wept to be recited to. Both are part of being a reciter.

And this closes a week of early believers: Mus'ab's short shroud, Zayd's name in the book, Usamah young and trusted, Umm Ayman the mother after a mother, Ja'far's two wings, Ibn Mas'ud the shepherd reciter, and now Ubayy.

how: Muslims remember Ubayy ibn Ka'b as a reciter and scribe of the Qur'an, and retell the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari in which the Prophet recited Surat al-Bayyinah to him at God's command.

o: a Meccan poet who mocked the early Muslims
a reciter of Medina the Prophet recited to
a companion who carried the banner at Badr

games.q: Ubayy ibn Ka'b — tap the pairs.
p: his answer to the Prophet's test

s: Ubayy asked the Prophet to recite to him
the Prophet said God had commanded him to recite to Ubayy.
Ubayy wept when he heard he was named
Bukhari says he asked 'did He name me?', was told yes, and wept.
Ubayy could not answer the Prophet's question about the verses
he answered Ayat al-Kursi, and the Prophet struck his chest: may knowledge delight you.

games.q: you are Ubayy. the Prophet tells you God has commanded him to recite a surah to you. what do you ask?
o: why me and not someone else?
games.why: Bukhari reports he asked 'did He name me?' and, told yes, wept.

practice: Think of one person you could share a short passage with, a friend, a sibling, a child at bedtime, and choose what it would be: a short surah, a line of a poem, a verse that matters to you.
Say it once in your mind, slowly, picturing their face as they hear it; you're not performing, you're carrying something to them by name. If you pray, you can ask that the words reach them well.

wordCard.voice: Ubayy, the reciter of Medina whom the Prophet was commanded to recite to, and who wept on hearing he had been named. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Ubayy, son of Ka'b, of the Ansar of Medina.

carryVoice: Your line: recite to him. Being named can move someone who already knows every word. A week of early believers, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4959 (God commanded me to recite to you Lam yakun; did He name me?; he wept)
Sahih Muslim 810 (which verse is greatest? Ayat al-Kursi; may knowledge delight you)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3758 (learn the Qur'an from four, including Ubayy ibn Ka'b)
